catalog_citation: Thomann, Georges. 1905. Essai de manuel de la langue néouolé parlée dans la partie occidentale de la Côte d'Ivoire. Paris: Ernest Leroux. (archive.org)
catalog_locator: Cinquième partie (Phraséologie et conversation), I. 'Accent', p. 105 (unnumbered page preceding p. 106); supporting footnote Première partie XXII 'La numération', p. 34 fn. 2
catalog_quote: En l'absence de tels moyens d'étude, il est difficile de déterminer les règles précises de l'accentuation d'une langue, surtout lorsqu'elle est aussi « chantée » que celle qui nous occupe. L'accent expiratoire, tel que nous le possédons dans les langues européennes, n'a, en effet, qu'une importance secondaire en néouolé et se confond en général avec un accent musical caractéristique qui suffit parfois seul à différencier un mot d'un autre; ainsi le mot ma, selon qu'il est prononcé sur une intonation ou une autre, signifie soit « maman » soit « banane ». Dans les mots disyllabiques cet accent est généralement placé sur la première syllabe; mais pour les mots plus longs, simples ou composés, les règles deviendraient compliquées et seraient traversées de nombreuses exceptions. La seconde méthode, qui peut-être est moins scientifique mais assurément plus simple et plus sûre, est d'apprendre l'accent sur place, par l'usage, en entendant parler les indigènes. Signalons toutefois, au sujet de l'accent, que le néouolé possède un accent de phrase placé généralement sur la dernière syllabe du dernier mot de chaque membre de phrase et surtout sur la particule exclamative a, chantée et nasillée, qui termine souvent les périodes.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.translation: Expiratory (stress) accent, such as we have it in European languages, has in fact only secondary importance in Neouole and generally merges with a characteristic musical accent which sometimes suffices by itself to distinguish one word from another; thus the word ma, depending on whether it is pronounced on one intonation or another, means either 'mother' or 'banana'. In disyllabic words this accent is generally placed on the first syllable; but for longer words, simple or compound, the rules would become complicated and would be crossed by numerous exceptions.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Pre-phonemic 1905 observer: Neyo is essentially tonal ('accent musical' distinguishes words); dynamic stress is weak and not clearly separable from tone; in disyllables the (stress/pitch) prominence is generally on the first syllable; no rule given for longer words.
new_statements.exceptions: Longer (tri-/polysyllabic, compound) words: author declines to state a rule, saying rules would be complicated with many exceptions. Modern sources (Vogler 2017 citing Grah 1983; fr.wikipedia citing Grah) describe Neyo as a three-level tone language and say nothing about stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level remark for disyllables; separately the author notes a phrase accent: 'le néouolé possède un accent de phrase placé généralement sur la dernière syllabe du dernier mot de chaque membre de phrase et surtout sur la particule exclamative a' (same page). The author explicitly conflates stress with tone ('se confond.. avec un accent musical'), so 'first syllable' may partly reflect tonal/pitch prominence.
new_statements.identity_note: Thomann 1905 describes 'néouolé', the language of the 'Néyau' of Sassandra = Neyo (neyo1238, ISO ney); same variety Grah 1983 calls níwɔ̄lī. No dialect specified (Vogler notes Grah counts 7 Neyo dialects).

new_statements.translation: Expiratory accent, as we have it in the European languages, is in fact only of secondary importance in Néouolé and generally merges with a characteristic musical accent which is sometimes enough on its own to distinguish one word from another; thus the word ma, depending on which intonation it is pronounced with, means either 'mother' or 'banana'. In disyllabic words this accent is generally placed on the first syllable; but for longer words, simple or compound, the rules would become complicated and would be crossed by numerous exceptions. [...] Néouolé has a phrase accent generally placed on the last syllable of the last word of each phrase member.

new_statements.relation_note: Same passage and same reading as the existing statement (tone language with a stress statement); the catalog record for Néouolé has an empty rule, so this refines it with the content: tonal, secondary expiratory stress initial in disyllables, phrase-final phrase accent. The HathiTrust copy hvd.hx51fz itself could not be downloaded (babel.hathitrust.org: an automated-access block 403 on the page view, 'Blocked from HathiTrust' 403 on the plaintext endpoint, not reachable by automated download), but the catalog API confirms it is the same 1905 edition (Harvard copy, pdus, Full view), which is held by the project as the IA scan and was read there, with the quote checked against the page scan.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word-level prominence is primarily tonal ('accent musical' distinguishes ma 'mother' vs 'banana'; preface p. III: gou 'flee'/'illness'/'salt' differ only by the note they are sung on). Expiratory (dynamic) stress is secondary; where noted, it falls on the first syllable of disyllables (also p. 34 fn. 2: 'Appuyer toujours sur la première voyelle des noms de nombre dissyllabiques'), with no rule given for longer words. A separate phrase accent falls on the last syllable of the last word of each phrase member, especially the exclamative particle a.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed at word level; a phrase-final accent on the last syllable of each phrase member is described separately (p. 105).
new_statements.exceptions: For words longer than two syllables 'the rules would become complicated and crossed by numerous exceptions'; p. 34 fn. 3: never stress the y in blèghe, ghefro, ghàso, ghàta (numerals); scattered vocabulary notes '(ne pas appuyer sur..)'.
new_statements.identity_note: Thomann describes the Néouolé (Néyau/Neyo) of the western Côte d'Ivoire coast, i.e. neyo1238 itself; the on-disk Vogler 2024 ms. (not in the work list) confirms Neyo has a three-register tone system, from Grah 1983, with nothing on stress.
